conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m so glad you’re here. I know the first weeks and months with a new baby can feel like a roller-coaster of emotions and exhaustion, and it’s completely normal to wonder, “Is what I’m feeling just the baby blues, or something more?”  

Today I’ll be guiding us through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a simple set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. Everything you share is confidential, and our goal is to make sure you feel heard, supported, and safe.  

We’ll take it one question at a time. If any feeling is hard to put into words, just describe it the best you can. Ready to begin?

**Question 1**  
In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

(soft sigh)  
I’ve still laughed a little—like when my husband sent that silly meme—but it feels muted. Most of the time it seems hard to find things genuinely funny the way I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I’ve laughed a couple of times, but it feels kind of forced, like I’m going through the motions. Most days it’s honestly hard to find anything really funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still get little sparks of excitement—like when my mom said she’d come over so I could take a walk—but they’re pretty rare. Mostly I don’t look forward to much anymore; even the stuff I used to enjoy feels kind of flat.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not a good enough mom. Even little things, like forgetting to pack an extra onesie, leave me feeling like I’ve failed.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my mind races—what if she spits up and chokes when I’m not looking, what if her breathing sounds weird, what if I’m missing something the doctor would catch. There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just keep spinning.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week—like yesterday when she was napping in the bassinet—I suddenly felt my heart racing and this wave of dread, almost like something awful was about to happen even though everything was quiet and fine. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Dishes pile up, the baby needs me, I haven’t showered, and it all feels like too much. I manage to push through, but it’s exhausting and I end up in tears at least once or twice a week.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t quiet—kept replaying every little thing I might’ve messed up with her. I finally drift off, then wake up at 2 or 3 a.m. with my heart pounding and can’t get back to sleep for an hour or more.
I have felt sad or miserable
Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud—I’ll be holding her and still feel hollow inside. Some moments are okay, but the sadness keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was when she wouldn’t stop crying and I couldn’t soothe her—I just sat on the nursery floor with tears running down, feeling like I’m failing her. Another time it hit out of nowhere while I was folding her laundry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

(quiet voice) Once or twice, like a quick flash—what if I just wasn’t here anymore—but I push it away. I don’t have any plan or real wish to do it; it’s more like my brain throws it out when everything feels too heavy.

You've shared that over the past two weeks laughter feels forced and rare, sparks of enjoyment are fleeting, and most days carry a heavy cloud of sadness and self-blame. You describe daily <sym>anxiety</sym> with racing thoughts about your baby's safety, sudden <sym>panic</sym> episodes, middle-of-the-night waking with a pounding heart, and moments of tearfully feeling you're failing your little one. You also mentioned fleeting thoughts of not wanting to be here, though you quickly push them away. These feelings are understandably overwhelming, and you deserve support and relief.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter feels forced and rare, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports rare sparks of excitement but overall significant reduction in anticipatory enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports blaming herself "a lot" and feeling like a failure over minor issues, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily anxiety with intrusive catastrophic thoughts during routine care, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic symptoms (heart racing, dread, shakiness) occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and tears but still managing to push through, aligning with "sometimes not coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to distressing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day" with persistent feelings of hollowness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "a couple of times" this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 on the EPDS places you well above the ≥14 threshold that signals probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse key criteria: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, recurrent thoughts of death, and sleep disturbance. The presence of <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> (Q10 ≥1) mandates immediate safety assessment per guideline. Combined with prominent <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym>, this pattern is consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depression and co-occurring <med>anxiety disorder</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health specialist for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Develop a written postpartum safety plan that includes 24/7 support contacts (partner, family, national maternal mental-health hotline 1-833-943-5746)
3. Discuss evidence-based treatments: <med>CBT</med>-based <med>interpersonal therapy</med> for perinatal depression, possible <med>sertraline</med> if indicated, and mother-infant dyadic supports
4. Begin gentle behavioural activation: 10-minute daily outdoor walk while a trusted adult cares for baby; schedule pleasurable micro-activities to counter <sym>anhedonia</sym>
5. Prioritise 4-hour uninterrupted night sleep block: express milk or use formula for one night feed so you can obtain restorative rest
6. Ask your clinician about local <med>PPD</med> support groups and home-visit nursing services for extra help with infant care while you recover
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2 wks post-delivery

Presenting symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily crying spells  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding parenting adequacy  
- Recurrent intrusive worries, panic episodes (no external trigger)  
- Middle insomnia with rumination; feels “drowning” in routine tasks  
- Passive self-harm cognition (no plan, intent, or preparatory behavior)

Pattern  
Consistent across all EPDS-equivalent items; symptoms present “pretty much every day” and interfere with basic functioning. No reported mania, psychosis, or substance use.

Screening significance  
High likelihood score for major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; safety flash (passive suicidal ideation) warrants immediate risk assessment and protective planning.

Next step  
Recommend same-day clinician review, formal EPDS scoring, safety plan, and consideration of expedited referral to perinatal mental-health specialty services.
